info.subtitle: Screening for Cognitive Impairment During Sleep Studies
info.description:
This is the **small version** of the training set for the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2026.

For the **large version**, please visit [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/physionet/physionetchallenge2026datalargeversion](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/physionet/physionetchallenge2026datalargeversion).

# Description

The [George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2026](https://physionetchallenges.org/2026/) uses large-scale sleep study data from the [Human Sleep Project](https://bdsp.io/content/hsp/2.0/), which aggregates real-world clinical polysomnography (PSG) recordings from multiple U.S. medical centers. These overnight sleep studies capture synchronized physiological signals spanning brain activity, eye movements, muscle tone, breathing, and cardiac function, along with detailed annotations of sleep stages and sleep-related events. All data are fully de-identified and shared under approved ethical protocols, while preserving the natural heterogeneity of clinical sleep studies.

Each PSG recording includes signals that reflect different aspects of physiology. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures changes in brain activity and sleep depth, electrooculography (EOG) identifies eye movements and REM sleep, electromyography (EMG) reflects muscle tone and movement, electrocardiography (ECG) characterizes heart rate and autonomic regulation, and respiratory effort and airflow signals describe breathing patterns and disruptions during sleep. Together, these modalities provide a comprehensive view of brain-body function during sleep.

Sleep stages and clinical event markers in this dataset are provided through two complementary sources. First, the [Complete AI Sleep Report (CAISR)] (https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article-abstract/48/8/zsaf134/8173031?redirectedFrom=fulltext) generates automated, high-fidelity annotations of sleep stages, arousals, respiratory events, and limb movements, following American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guidelines. These algorithmic annotations are available for the training, validation, and test sets. Second, the training data also include human-scored annotations produced by trained sleep technicians, who manually labeled sleep stages and clinical events according to the same AASM standards. This dual-annotation framework enables direct comparison between automated and expert human scoring.

The training set consists of recordings from three U.S. clinical sites. The validation and test sets are hidden and originate from sites distinct from those in the training data, enabling a realistic cross-site evaluation that reflects real-world deployment and rigorously assesses model generalizability. To support development, we additionally provide ten example recordings from each of the two hidden sites; however, these samples are not part of the official validation or test sets.

The outcome of interest in this challenge is whether an individual later develops mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease, or dementia. Subtle disruptions in sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, or respiration may emerge years before clinical symptoms, making sleep a promising early indicator of cognitive decline.

The [George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2026](https://physionetchallenges.org/2026/) leverages this potential by inviting teams to analyze PSG recordings to identify individuals at risk for future cognitive impairment. For additional details on the dataset, annotations, and challenge structure, please refer to the [PhysioNet Challenge website](https://physionetchallenges.org/2026/).

info.userSpecifiedSources: The dataset originates from the Human Sleep Project, which integrates clinical polysomnography (PSG) recordings from five U.S. institutions: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), Emory University, Kaiser Permanente, Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB), and Stanford University. All data were de-identified according to HIPAA Safe Harbor standards and made publicly accessible under an approved IRB protocol (BIDMC IRB #2022P000417). Only the first PSG session per participant was included, and personal identifiers were replaced with random IDs. For participants older than 89 years, age was capped at 90, and dates were randomly shifted ±365 days.
